strengths: Introduces a simple and memory-efficient alternative to the binary target-based/target-free choice by sharing all feature-extractor parameters and freezing only a copy of the last linear head as the target.
Leverages iterated Q-learning with multiple linear heads to learn consecutive Bellman iterations in parallel, reducing the performance gap between target-free and target-based methods.
Evaluates across online Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm, and offline CQL, using IQM and AUC with bootstrap confidence intervals.
Shows concrete gains: iS-DQN K=9 outperforms target-based DQN by 6% AUC on CNN+LN and closes the gap in other settings, while using roughly half the parameters of target-based DQN.
Provides useful analysis of why the method helps: gradient cosine similarity to target-based DQN, higher effective rank, and fewer dormant neurons.
Demonstrates generality of the shared-feature idea through an ensemble variant (ES-CQL) and positions the method as orthogonal to existing target-free regularization techniques.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameters, architecture descriptions, game selection, and a promise to release code.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: it combines existing iterated Q-learning with a simple shared-feature/frozen-head target mechanism, without new theoretical guarantees or convergence analysis for the shared-feature iterated target.

Evaluation is limited to Atari discrete control; no continuous-control or other domains are tested, and there is no empirical comparison to other strong target-free methods despite claiming orthogonality.
The claim of comparable training time is not supported by wall-clock, VRAM, or compute measurements; only parameter counts are reported.

K is an additional hyperparameter, and the optimal value varies substantially across architectures (3, 9, 49), with performance degrading for large K in some settings; sensitivity analysis is limited.

Some algorithmic details are unclear or underspecified, especially the interaction between shared features, target parameters, and the chain-enforcement update; the pseudo-code does not explicitly handle target parameter copies.
Statistical robustness is limited: 5 seeds per game and 10-15 games, with some appendix results showing overlapping confidence intervals, so not all reported gains are clearly significant.
The paper does not compare against several relevant target-free or regularization baselines in the online discrete setting, leaving the empirical positioning incomplete.

strengths: The proposed method is simple and practical: sharing all features while keeping only the final linear layer as a target head substantially reduces the memory overhead of target networks.

The paper evaluates the idea across several Atari settings, including online and offline RL, two architectures (CNN and IMPALA), multiple K values, and uses IQM/AUC with confidence intervals, which is stronger than a single-setting evaluation.
The diagnostic analyses on gradient cosine similarity and effective rank provide some insight into why the shared-head design may stabilize learning.
Reproducibility is relatively good: hyperparameters and experiment setup are detailed, and the code is promised to be open-sourced.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method combines two existing ideas—using only the last layer as a frozen target and iterated Q-learning—with no theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees. The core contribution is an incremental architectural modification.

A critical baseline is missing: the direct predecessor, iterated Q-Network (Vincent et al., 2025), is not compared against. Without this, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from iterated Q-learning versus the shared-head parameterization.

The target-free baselines are weak and narrow: the paper mainly compares against vanilla target-free DQN/CQL, while other target-free regularization methods (e.g., MellowMax, CrossQ, Fourier features) are discussed but not evaluated in the main experiments. Claims about improving target-free RL broadly are therefore under-supported.

The claim of comparable training time is not backed by wall-clock measurements or throughput numbers; only parameter counts are shown. Memory savings in practice may differ from parameter-count savings.

The evaluation is confined to discrete-action Atari with DQN/CQL-style algorithms. Generalization to continuous control, different value-based methods, or more modern RL baselines is not demonstrated.
Hyperparameter and K sensitivity is not adequately addressed. Performance varies non-monotonically with K across architectures, and there is no principled guidance for choosing K.

The paper positions the method as bridging target-free and target-based RL, but the proposed algorithm still relies on a frozen, periodically updated target head, so it is not target-free. The framing overstates the conceptual shift from prior work.

Some central claims rely on relatively small or overlapping confidence intervals, and the analysis is post hoc; stronger statistical evidence would be needed to support claims such as outperforming target-based DQN by 6%.

strengths: Proposes a simple and effective method to mitigate the performance drop of target-free value-based RL by sharing the feature extractor with the online network and using only frozen linear head(s) as lightweight target(s).
Extends the approach to iterated Q-learning with multiple linear heads, learning consecutive Bellman iterations in parallel while keeping memory close to target-free methods.

Provides a thorough empirical evaluation across online and offline Atari, CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm, and with CQL; uses AUC, IQM, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals with 5 seeds.
Demonstrates clear memory advantages: iS-QN uses roughly half the parameters of target-based DQN while outperforming target-free DQN, and even K=49 remains far below target-based memory.
Includes useful mechanistic insights via gradient cosine similarity and effective rank, showing that iS-QN brings learning dynamics and representation capacity closer to target-based training.
Good reproducibility practices: code to be open-sourced, standard hyperparameters kept fixed, detailed appendix on game selection and metrics.
weaknesses: No theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees for the proposed method with nonlinear function approximation; the contribution is primarily empirical.
Evaluation is limited to discrete-action Atari domains; continuous control is left to future work, and offline evaluation only uses CQL.

Missing direct comparisons to target-based iterated Q-Network (i-QN) and to other recent target-free regularization methods (e.g., MellowMax, CrossQ, Fourier features), despite claiming orthogonality to such methods; only LayerNorm is combined with iS-QN.
The abstract claims comparable training time, but the paper reports parameter counts rather than actual wall-clock or computational training-time measurements.
Performance is not monotonic in K (e.g., K=49 degrades with CNN+LayerNorm, and K>3 degrades without LayerNorm), so K requires tuning and no principled selection strategy is provided.
Some explanations are intuitive rather than rigorously validated, e.g., the claim that target-free methods traverse Bellman iterations too quickly and therefore become unstable.

strengths: Simple and practical method that reduces the memory footprint of target networks by sharing all but the last linear layer between online and target networks, enabling resource-efficient RL.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse domains: online discrete control (Atari with CNN/IMPALA), offline discrete control (CQL), continuous control (SAC/SimbaV2), and language-based RL (ILQL/Wordle).

Strong and consistent results: iS-QN substantially narrows or closes the performance gap between target-free and target-based methods, and sometimes outperforms target-based baselines while using approximately half the Q-network parameters.
Provides useful analysis of why the method works, including gradient similarity, target churn, and effective rank, which helps explain the improved stability and representation quality.
Good reproducibility practices: hyperparameters are listed, individual learning curves are provided, and code is promised upon acceptance.
weaknesses: The core idea is incremental: it combines shared-feature target construction with the existing iterated Q-learning framework. Novelty may be considered modest for a top-tier venue.

The iterated Q-learning interpretation is approximate: for heads k>1, the target Q_{k-1} is updated concurrently within each T-step window rather than being held fixed, so targets are not fully delayed as in standard iterated Q-learning. This may weaken the theoretical grounding.
The number of Bellman iterations K is a new hyperparameter with different optimal values per setting, and the paper does not provide a principled way to choose it.

Comparisons to other target-free stabilization methods (e.g., DeepMellow, Fourier features, functional regularization) are not empirically included, despite the claim that the approach is orthogonal to such techniques.

Some experimental choices are inconsistent across algorithms (e.g., BatchNorm used for TF-SAC and iS-SAC but not TB-SAC), which could affect fairness of comparisons, although the authors justify it empirically.
No formal convergence or theoretical guarantees are provided; the contribution is primarily empirical.

strengths: Introduces a simple and memory-efficient alternative to standard target networks by storing only the last linear layer as a frozen target head while sharing feature extractor parameters with the online network.
Extends iterated Q-learning to the shared-feature setting, allowing multiple Bellman iterations to be learned in parallel with only a small number of additional head parameters.
Provides a broad empirical study across online discrete control, offline RL, continuous control, and language-based RL, using several architectures and datasets.
Reproducibility is strong: code release is promised, hyperparameters are listed, multiple seeds and individual learning curves are reported, and IQM/bootstrap confidence intervals are used.
Includes some useful analysis of gradient similarity, target churn, and effective rank, offering insight into why the shared-head target may improve over purely target-free training.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method mainly combines existing iterated Q-learning with a shared feature extractor and a copied final linear head. There is no theoretical grounding or convergence analysis.

Baselines are limited to vanilla target-based and target-free versions of the same algorithms. Recent target-free or regularization-based methods cited in related work (e.g., MellowMax, CrossQ-style approaches) are not empirically compared, despite claims that the method is orthogonal to them.

The central claim of bridging the target-free/target-based gap is only partially supported. Offline iS-CQL still remains below the target-based method, DMC iS-SAC with K=9 is only on par with K=1 and overlaps the target-based method, and Wordle target-free ILQL is already close to target-based ILQL.

K is a new hyperparameter whose optimal value varies substantially across settings (K=1 to K=49). The paper tunes K per benchmark while claiming standard hyperparameters, which weakens the strength and generality of the empirical conclusions.

Sharing features means target values still change with every online feature update; the target churn is only intermediate between target-free and target-based. Thus the method does not fully recover target-based stability, despite positioning itself as leveraging target-network literature.

Evaluation focuses on AUC rather than final performance or robustness, and there is little ablation on the multi-head loss aggregation, target update schedule, or the interaction between K and architecture/regularization, making the source of gains somewhat unclear.

strengths: Simple and practical memory-efficient design: freezing only the final linear layer as a target network while sharing the feature extractor with the online network reduces Q-network parameter footprint substantially across settings.
Effectively combines iterated Q-learning with shared targets, allowing multiple Bellman updates to be learned in parallel and improving sample efficiency of target-free methods.

Broad empirical validation across online/offline discrete control, continuous control, and language-based RL; includes multiple architectures (CNN, IMPALA, SimbaV2, GPT-2) and robust IQM/AUC statistics with confidence intervals.

Demonstrates closing or reversing the target-free vs. target-based performance gap in many settings; K=1 already helps, and larger K sometimes outperforms target-based methods while using roughly half the Q-network parameters.
Approach is orthogonal and compatible with normalization techniques and existing methods; the ES-CQL variant shows that shared-feature targets are not limited to iterated Q-learning.
Provides useful diagnostics: gradient similarity to target-based learning, target churn, effective rank, and dormant neurons help explain stabilization and representation gains.
Reproducibility is strong: code, detailed hyperparameters, and individual learning curves are provided.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines prior iterated Q-learning with a shared last-layer target network, and lacks theoretical convergence or stability guarantees.
K is a new and setting-dependent hyperparameter; the optimal value varies by environment/architecture, and performance can decline for large K, with no principled selection rule.

The shared target is not truly stationary because the feature extractor updates at every gradient step; stability is supported empirically but not theoretically, and may depend on normalization choices.

Results are not uniformly better: in continuous control, iS-SAC K=9 is on par with K=1; in Wordle, target-free is not significantly worse; some games show no consistent gain, so the 'bridging' claim is somewhat overstated.

Memory savings apply only to Q-network parameters; replay buffer, optimizer states, activations, and inference memory are unchanged, and training time/FLOPs are often similar to target-based approaches.

AUC is normalized by target-based performance, and baseline architectures are modified with LayerNorm/BatchNorm in some cases but not others, which may complicate absolute interpretation and generalization.
No empirical integration with pruning/quantization is provided; comparisons to some relevant target-free regularization methods are discussed but not exhaustively evaluated.

strengths: Simple and practical idea: using only a copied last linear layer as the target while sharing all other features substantially reduces the memory footprint compared with standard target networks.
Extends naturally to iterated Q-learning with multiple heads (iS-QN), improving sample efficiency of target-free methods without greatly increasing parameters.

Extensive empirical evaluation across online discrete control (Atari with CNN/IMPALA), offline RL (CQL), continuous control (SAC/SimbaV2), language-based RL (ILQL/Wordle), and streaming RL (Stream Q(λ)).
Uses robust evaluation metrics (IQM, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, normalized AUC) and reports multiple seeds across most settings.
Provides useful mechanistic analyses, including gradient cosine similarity to target-based learning, target churn, and effective rank, which support the empirical claims.
Includes relevant ablations on the number of Bellman iterations K, target-update period, feature width, meta-gradient weighting, and mixed-precision training.
Reproducibility is addressed with hyperparameter tables, implementation details, and a carbon-impact statement.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method combines shared-feature targets with iterated Q-learning, both of which build heavily on existing work, without introducing a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

There is no theoretical convergence or stability analysis. Because the target network is not fully frozen — the shared torso changes at every gradient step — standard target-network stability arguments do not directly apply.

Main experiments mostly compare against target-free and target-based versions of the same base algorithms rather than strong recent target-free methods such as CrossQ or other regularization-based approaches; the broader competitiveness of iS-QN is therefore not fully established.

K is introduced as a sensitive new hyperparameter with different optimal values across settings (e.g., K=9 for CNN Atari, K=49 for IMPALA, K=3 for streaming), and gains are limited in some settings (e.g., iS-SAC K=9 performs on par with K=1).

Some claims are setting-dependent: the method does not always bridge the gap to target-based methods (e.g., streaming RL improves over target-free but not necessarily over target-based), and without LayerNorm the gap is reduced but not eliminated.
The algorithm description around updating heads via ω_k ← ω_{k+1} and the precise distinction between online and target heads is somewhat confusing and could be clarified to avoid ambiguity.

Baseline comparisons may be weakened by using target-free baselines that are not state-of-the-art in all domains, making it difficult to isolate how much of the gain comes from the proposed sharing mechanism versus stronger normalization or implementation choices.

strengths: The proposed idea is simple and intuitive: share all features between online and target networks while keeping only a copy of the last linear layer, which can substantially reduce memory dedicated to Q-network parameters.

The empirical study is broad, covering online Atari with two architectures, offline CQL, continuous-control SAC, language-based ILQL, and streaming RL, with useful use of IQM, confidence intervals, and normalized AUC.
The paper provides several analyses (gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank, ablations on K and target update period) that attempt to explain why the method helps.
Reproducibility is well addressed: code is provided, hyperparameters are listed, carbon impact is reported, and individual learning curves are included.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The work combines existing ingredients: target networks for the last layer, feature sharing between online and target networks, and iterated Q-learning from Vincent et al. (2025b). The core contribution is an incremental engineering modification rather than a fundamentally new RL algorithm.

The algorithmic description of iS-QN is technically unclear and potentially flawed. In the loss, Q_k regresses a stop-gradient Q_{k-1}, but Q_{k-1} is itself an online head updated by its own loss except for Q_0. Thus, for K > 1, most targets are not delayed target networks; they change at every gradient step. The periodic update ω_k ← ω_{k+1} does not properly create the target-network structure of iterated Q-learning. This casts doubt on the claim that the method faithfully leverages target-based stabilization.

There is no theoretical analysis of convergence, stability, or bias. The post-hoc metrics in Section 5.6 are correlational and do not justify why the proposed mechanism should work or when it will fail.

Evaluation has important weaknesses. Target-free baselines are trained with the same hyperparameters as target-based versions, which may under-tune them; improvements are inconsistent across settings (e.g., in DMC, iS-SAC K=9 only performs on par with K=1; on Wordle target-free is not significantly worse than target-based; in streaming, large K hurts). Some claims rely on overlapping confidence intervals.

The paper overclaims relative to the evidence. It states that iS-QN 'bridges the performance gap' broadly, but in continuous control the iterated component provides no improvement over the shared-features K=1 variant, and in some settings the target-free gap is small or absent. The main benefits often come from the shared last-layer target alone, not from iterated Q-learning.

Missing comparisons to other target-free or memory-efficient methods (e.g., CrossQ, DroQ, other regularized target-free approaches) weaken the empirical positioning. The paper argues orthogonality but does not directly test against these methods.

Practical memory savings may be less impactful than implied, since optimizer states, replay buffer, and activations can dominate training memory. The paper acknowledges this only in limitations, but the abstract and introduction emphasize low memory footprint strongly.

Hyperparameter sensitivity remains a concern: optimal K varies significantly across settings, and the recommended heuristic ('increase K until performance drops') is expensive and not always reliable. Some design choices (head sampling, loss scaling in continuous control) appear heuristic and are not fully studied.

strengths: Introduces a simple yet effective method (iS-QN) that combines shared features with iterated Q-learning to reduce the memory footprint of target-based RL while improving sample efficiency.

Extensive empirical evaluation across diverse settings: online discrete control (Atari with CNN and IMPALA), offline discrete control (CQL), online continuous control (DMC with SAC), language-based RL (Wordle with ILQL), and streaming RL (Stream Q(λ)).
Clear memory reduction: the method uses a single Q-network with linear heads, achieving comparable or better performance with roughly half the parameters of target-based approaches.
Insightful analysis: gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank, and dormant neuron measurements provide understanding of why the method stabilizes learning and improves representation.
Good reproducibility: code, hyperparameters, and experimental setup are detailed; carbon impact and LLM usage are disclosed.
Orthogonal to existing regularization techniques, demonstrated by improving target-free methods equipped with MellowMax, LayerNorm, BatchNorm, etc.
Broad relevance to resource-efficient reinforcement learning, with potential impact on both discrete and continuous control domains.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea of sharing features with a frozen last linear layer as target and combining with iterated Q-learning builds heavily on existing work (e.g., Vincent et al. 2025b, shared feature targets). The contribution is more empirical than conceptual.

Introduces a new hyperparameter K, with optimal value varying across settings and no principled selection method. The meta-gradient approach in the appendix learns equal weights and does not solve selection.
Lack of theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees; the paper is purely empirical, which limits depth of understanding.
In continuous control, iS-SAC K=9 performs on par with K=1 and only overlaps with TB-SAC; the benefit of multiple heads is less clear in this setting, and the paper does not fully resolve why.

Some experimental comparisons may be confounded: in continuous control, BatchNorm is used for TF and iS but not TB, so the performance gap could partly reflect normalization rather than target network removal. The paper acknowledges this but it complicates interpretation.
